title: NHL Award Futures 2026-27: Where Canadians Find Value
excerpt: Training camps are opening. Here is how Canadian bettors should approach Hart, Vezina, Norris and Calder futures for 2026-27, and where the value hides.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Training camps open this month, and with them comes the annual flood of NHL award futures. Hart, Vezina, Norris, Calder, Selke — every sportsbook serving Canadian players will have a board up within days, and most of it will be priced on last season's narrative rather than this season's likely voting. For bettors willing to do a little homework, NHL award futures are one of the few corners of the hockey market where public perception and actual voting behaviour drift far enough apart to create genuine value.

This guide walks through how each major award is actually decided, where the pricing tends to go wrong, and how to size a futures position so it does not quietly eat your bankroll for eight months.

Why NHL award futures are priced loosely

Sportsbooks price game markets with enormous precision because they take huge volume on them and can adjust in real time. Award futures are different. They attract modest handle, they sit open for months, and the outcome depends on a vote by the Professional Hockey Writers' Association rather than on anything measurable on the ice. Books are not modelling a hundred writers' preferences; they are anchoring on last year's result, on point projections, and on whatever names the hockey media has been talking about in August.

That creates soft spots. A player who finished fourth in Hart voting last year will be priced near the top of the board regardless of whether his team's situation improved or deteriorated. A goaltender on a bad defensive team will be priced out of Vezina contention even if his individual numbers are elite. These are not exploitable every year, but the errors are systematic enough to look for.

As always, the first practical step is line shopping. Award futures vary wildly between books — it is routine to find one operator offering a contender at meaningfully longer odds than another because their liability is sitting elsewhere. Holding accounts at two or three licensed sites is the cheapest edge available, and our Canadian sportsbook rankings lay out which books offer the deepest futures boards.

The Hart Trophy: narrative plus team success

The Hart goes to the player judged most valuable to his team, and the voting record is clear about what that means in practice: the winner is usually a high-scoring forward on a team that makes the playoffs comfortably, and very often the league's leading scorer or close to it.

Two filters cut most of the board:

  • Team quality. Voters rarely reward a spectacular individual season on a team that misses the playoffs. If you cannot see a path to a top-three divisional finish, the price is usually too short regardless of talent.
  • Position. Defencemen and goaltenders win the Hart occasionally, but the base rate is low enough that long odds on them are almost never long enough.

The value play in Hart markets is typically a centre in the 20-to-40 range on the board who is entering his prime, has an improved supporting cast, and plays on a team the projection models like more than the public does. Those bets lose most years. When they hit, they pay for a lot of losing tickets.

The Vezina: a general managers' vote

The Vezina is the one major award voted on by the league's general managers rather than the writers, and that distinction matters more than most bettors realise. GMs tend to reward workload and win totals. A goaltender who plays 60-plus games on a strong team is the archetype; a spectacular part-time performer in a tandem is the classic trap.

Before backing a goalie, ask three questions. Is he the clear starter, or will he split the crease? Does the team in front of him suppress shot quality? And is the backup good enough that the coach will happily rest him in March? Tandem hockey has quietly destroyed a lot of Vezina tickets over the last several seasons, and the market has not fully adjusted to how few goaltenders now carry a genuine workhorse load.

Norris and Selke: the repeat-winner effect

Both the Norris and the Selke show strong incumbency. Voters return to familiar names, and a defenceman or defensive forward who has finished top-three before starts with an enormous reputational head start. That makes long-shot value scarce but also makes the favourites less overpriced than they look. If a repeat contender is available at a price close to the field, that is often the sober play.

The Calder: the one market worth real attention

Rookie of the Year is where Canadian bettors should concentrate their research, because it is the award most sensitive to information that is publicly available in September and most likely to be mispriced in the process.

The Calder is won by ice time. A rookie who opens the season in a top-six forward role or a top-four defensive pairing has a structural advantage over a more talented player buried on the fourth line or sent down for a conditioning stint. Preseason is genuinely useful here: line combinations in mid-September often preview the opening-night deployment, and books are slow to reprice rookie markets on camp news.

A few principles that hold up well:

  • Favour forwards over defencemen — the raw point totals that drive voting are easier to accumulate up front.
  • Favour rookies on rebuilding teams that have every incentive to play them heavy minutes and run them on the power play.
  • Be wary of European and college signings whose contracts allow a minor-league start.
  • Check waiver eligibility. A player who can be sent down without clearing waivers is a genuine roster risk.

If you are newer to futures markets and want a refresher on how long-term odds and payouts work, our sports betting basics guide covers odds formats and bet types before you commit money for a season.

Sizing, timing and the cost of tied-up money

The hidden cost of any futures bet is opportunity cost. Money placed on a Hart ticket in September is unavailable until April, and you cannot compound it, hedge it cheaply, or adjust it when circumstances change. That argues for keeping total futures exposure small — a single-digit percentage of your bankroll across the entire board, not per bet.

Timing matters too. Award prices generally shorten on the players who start hot, which means there is usually a better entry point for a specific name in late October than in mid-September. The exception is the Calder, where camp news moves prices quickly and waiting can cost you the number entirely.

Finally, resist the urge to build a portfolio of ten long shots. Futures boards are heavily juiced — the sum of implied probabilities across an award market is often well over 100% — so every additional ticket you add increases your exposure to that built-in margin. Two or three well-reasoned positions beat a scattergun.

Getting set for the season

Award futures are entertainment with a real edge attached, provided you treat them as a small slice of a broader betting plan rather than the plan itself. Shop every price, understand who votes for what, concentrate your effort on the Calder where information is genuinely actionable, and keep your stakes modest enough that an eight-month wait does not hurt.
